articles.title: Microsoft is laying off as many as 9,000 employees
articles.summary: Microsoft’s latest job cuts come after multiple rounds of layoffs over the past year.
articles.body: Microsoft confirmed that it’s laying off as many as 9,100 employees, or about 4 percent of its workforce, in yet another round of cuts this year, reports The Seattle Times. Employees in Microsoft’s Xbox division, known as Microsoft Gaming, are being hit hard by these layoffs, although exact numbers and divisions are not yet known. Xbox leader Phil Spencer said in a message to the team, “To position Gaming for enduring success and allow us to focus on strategic growth areas, we will end or decrease work in certain areas of the business and follow Microsoft’s lead in removing layers of management to increase agility and effectiveness.” Bloomberg reports that the now Microsoft-owned King division that makes Candy Crush is cutting about 10 percent of employees, or 200 people, while other units, like ZeniMax, have also confirmed they are cutting jobs. Microsoft is also laying off more than 70 people at its Forza Motorsport studio, Turn 10, as well as cancelling its Perfect Dark and Everwild games. The studio behind Perfect Dark, The Initiative, is also closing down as part of these layoffs. These major layoffs come less than two months after Microsoft announced it was cutting more than 6,000 employees, followed by an additional 305 reductions in early June. Microsoft employees have faced a series of layoffs over the past year, including a round of performance-based cuts that have seriously hit morale, according to multiple Microsoft employees I’ve spoken to. Microsoft laid off 1,900 Activision Blizzard and Xbox employees in January 2024, followed by several game studio closures and job losses in May, and 1,000 job losses from its HoloLens and Azure cloud teams in June. Microsoft also laid off 650 more Xbox employees in September, as part of a restructuring related to the company’s acquisition of Activision Blizzard. This is the memo that Xbox boss Phil Spencer sent to employees: > Today we are sharing decisions that will impact colleagues across our organization. To position Gaming for enduring success and allow us to focus on strategic growth areas, we will end or decrease work in certain areas of the business and follow Microsoft’s lead in removing layers of management to increase agility and effectiveness. Out of respect for those impacted today, the specifics of today’s notifications and any organizational shifts will be shared by your team leaders in the coming days. > I recognize that these changes come at a time when we have more players, games, and gaming hours than ever before. Our platform, hardware, and game roadmap have never looked stronger. The success we’re seeing currently is based on tough decisions we’ve made previously. We must make choices now for continued success in future years and a key part of that strategy is the discipline to prioritize the strongest opportunities. We will protect what is thriving and concentrate effort on areas with the greatest potential, while delivering on the expectations the company has for our business. This focused approach means we can deliver exceptional games and experiences for players for generations to come. > Prioritizing our opportunities is essential, but that does not lessen the significance of this moment. Simply put, we would not be where we are today without the time, energy, and creativity of those whose roles are impacted. These decisions are not a reflection of the talent, creativity, and dedication of the people involved. Our momentum is not accidental—it is the result of years of dedicated effort from our teams. > HR is working directly with impacted employees to provide severance plan benefits (aligned with local laws), including pay, healthcare coverage, and job placement resources to support their transition. Employees whose roles were eliminated are encouraged to explore open positions across Microsoft Gaming, where their applications will be given priority review. > Thank you to everyone who has shaped our culture, our products, and our community. We will move forward with deep appreciation and respect for all who have contributed to this journey. > Phil Update, July 2nd: Article updated with more details on the Xbox layoffs.

articles.title: The Internet Reacts to the Cancellation of Mass Effect 5 and the Death of BioWare
articles.summary: The Internet Reacts to the Cancelation of Mass Effect 5 and the Death of BioWare.
articles.body:
On October 21, EA announced a major restructuring of its development studios and current projects, which included the closure of BioWare and the cancellation of the next Mass Effect game.

This news hit fans like a truck, as many were excitedly waiting for the next installment in the beloved sci-fi role-playing series. BioWare created some of the most beloved and influential RPGs in history over the course of 30 years of existence, but its closure was relegated to just a single paragraph in EA's memo to staff on today's dramatic company changes .

“As we focus on these larger opportunities, we've had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect. We've made the decision not to move forward with this development, which means we’re closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace. BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly,” Cam Weber, president and chief studios officer, and David Tinson, president and COO, said in the memo.

Needless to say, fans of BioWare games — particularly Mass Effect — were left devastated by this news. On social media, the prevailing sentiment seems to be one of anger and despair, with commenters venting their spleen at EA and the current state of the industry.

“I was so excited for N7 day. I was so excited for the next Mass Effect game. The Mass Effect trilogy is one of my favorite games of all time, and now it’s dead forever. I don’t even know what to think or say, everything feels unreal,” one fan wrote online.

“This is a f**king dagger in my heart. Thank you for being a huge part of my childhood,” another said .

“Please God, PLEASE sell your IPs to another company,” yet another urged . “Don't let the legacy of Mass Effect and Dragon Age die with these last gory gasps. Sell them to other companies that can continue telling the stories they can... Don't let EA hold these settings hostage.”

Prominent members of the video game development community also offered their thoughts. The co-CEO of The Witcher and Cyberpunk developer CD Projekt Red, Michal Nowakowski, weighed in with a statement honoring BioWare for its help and collaboration over the years.

“BioWare has been a massive part of CDPR history. We befriended them when localizing and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later, they were a great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3. I had the pleasure to visit them a few times in Edmonton and also host them in our Warsaw office. Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry,” he wrote .

Paweł Sasko, associate game director on Cyberpunk 2, said BioWare's Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 "shaped my imagination and the desire to create games." He continued: "I would have never been here without BioWare igniting the fire in my heart. It inspired me, formed me, enriched my imagination, and for that I will be forever grateful. I will always remember you."

inXile boss Brian Fargo, who founded Interplay Entertainment, called it a "sad day indeed." "I remember when BioWare was a small studio that made Shattered Steel for us at Interplay," he said. "We saw the promise in what they could do, and they went on to create Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 and become legendary. A sad day indeed. My thoughts are with everyone there today."

Swen Vincke, boss of Baldur's Gate 3 developer Larian, described BioWare's closure as "not something I ever expected to see."

"Larian and BioWare started their trajectories in the games industry at the same time and BioWare led the way in making RPGs big," he continued. "It's almost unimaginable that we're now entering an era were the name BioWare won't show up anymore when discussing upcoming RPGs. What a loss for all of us.

"Thank you for all the games. Thank you for the many hours of gameplay. Thank you for all the stories . You can be damned proud of what you achieved. I hope you all land well."

Thomas Puha, communications director at Alan Wake and Control developer Remedy, commented : "This was coming but so sad to read. The growing problem for large publishers is that smaller AAA games won’t bring enough money so can’t take the risk on them, but not doing original games? We need those, need new franchises."

Casey Hudson, the former BioWare GM, and director of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and the Mass Effect Trilogy, called it "sad news on multiple fronts - for those of us who worked there, for our friends and colleagues at BioWare who are impacted, and for fans who were looking forward to the next Mass Effect adventure.

"I started my career at BioWare and will forever be grateful to the founders, Greg and Ray, for inviting me to join in BioWare's legendary journey. Its legacy will live on through those who were part of it and continue to create games through a passion for unforgettable stories, worlds and characters."

Hudson is now CEO of Arcanaut Studios, which is developing a spiritual successor to KOTOR called Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic.

BioWare issued a statement of its own on social media, writing: “For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life. Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending.

“There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition. What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.”

Mike Gamble, executive producer of Mass Effect at BioWare, told fans in a social media post : "Your support has meant everything to me over the past 17 years at BioWare."

It’s been a tumultuous year for EA; in August, the company went private in a $55 billion acquisition to an investor group comprised of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners. The Financial Times reported that this deal hinged on the hope that AI would “significantly” cut EA’s operating costs, helping the consortium of private investors to better manage the debt they piled onto the game company.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: DC’s Clayface Turns a Tragic Batman Villain Origin Story Into a Fun, Visceral Body Horror Movie Throwback
articles.summary: Clayface is at its best when it embraces its B-movie absurdity. It’s a fun body horror romp that realizes its nasty potential in its final act after a slow-burn set-up.
articles.body:
Clayface opens in North America on October 23 and internationally on October 21.

It takes the film a while to find its groove, but once it does, Clayface delivers just the sort of nasty but fun body horror I was hoping it would.

Director James Watkins has fashioned a gritty throwback to not only the hardboiled revenge thrillers and low-budget horror flicks of the ‘50s and ‘60s but also to the cult classics of the ‘80s and ‘90s that paid homage to them. (Shades of The Fly, Darkman, and Johnny Handsome can all be found in Clayface.)

Based on the DC Comics character and working from a screenplay by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini, Clayface follows rising young movie star Matt Hagen ( Tom Rhys Harries ), a Gotham City native whose sketchy, hardscrabble background calls to mind that of Mark Wahlberg. Now a successful film actor, everything is going Matt’s way — until he runs afoul of Gotham’s most vicious and powerful crime lord, Markos Szabo (David Dencik), whose goons carve up Matt’s pretty boy face as punishment.

Disfigured and distraught, Matt finds no recourse from either the law or from multiple surgeries until he seeks out assistance from Dr. Caitlyn Corr ( Naomi Ackie ). Caitlyn’s similarly down on her luck, with her cutting edge research having been recently ripped off by her former partners. When Matt comes to her volunteering to be a human test subject for her experimental, AI-infused nanobot regenerative tech, she reluctantly says yes. All seems to be going well at first, but this movie ain’t called Clayface because Matt’s new skincare regimen worked out great.

DC Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

Harries has a young Malcolm McDowell quality to him, as in impish good looks that hint at an inner darkness. The actor never overplays his scenes despite there being plenty of opportunities for him to have gone big. As sympathetically played by Ackie, Caitlyn is more misguided than mad scientist despite being responsible for the physical monster Matt becomes. But while her nanobots have infiltrated and altered Matt, the film suggests they’ve merely unlocked and amplified a very bad side of him that was already there.

When Matt’s pursuit of his attackers and those who have betrayed him finally comes, it allows the film to finally embrace its inherent absurdity and capitalize on the nastiness it was keeping at bay while it was trying to make Matt sympathetic. Once Matt is no longer the victim and becomes the gooey Angel of Death we’ve been waiting for, the film gets a newfound jolt of energy and unleashes some of its most clever, thrilling and darkly funny sequences (following the earlier airplane bathroom scene seen in trailers and a creepy sleep study sequence).

Watkins has previously helmed genre films like The Woman in Black and Speak No Evil, in addition to the iconic “Shut Up and Dance” episode of Black Mirror. He and his creative team — including cinematographer Rob Hardy, production designer James Price, editor Jon Harris, Makeup Designer Nicole Stafford and Legacy Effects — make great use of Matt’s power to shapeshift, but also find the humor and tension in those situations, with Matt using his skills as an actor to literally inhabit a slew of different characters one after another.

As Matt’s condition worsens and his desire for revenge fully consumes him, he devolves morally and physically into something truly monstrous. Clayface’s comics and cartoon-accurate final form isn’t revealed until the film’s closing moments, but it effectively caps off Matt’s tragic downfall.

Although it carries the banner of James Gunn’s DC Studios, Clayface could just as easily have been set outside of the DCU. Aside from taking place in the DC Comics locations of Gotham City and Coast City, there’s nothing on display here that screams DC Comics. Still, Clayface proves that the DCU can offer more than just superhero fisticuffs and save-the-world plots. The question remains how large of an audience there will be for them.

Jim Vejvoda (he/him) is IGN's Assoc. Director of Entertainment Content.

articles.title: The Acer Nitro  RX 9060 XT Gaming PC Offers Great 1440p Gaming Performance for Just $1,200
articles.summary: The equipped Radeon RX 9060 XT GPU is the preferred 16GB variant.
articles.body:
If you're looking for a capable gaming PC at a solid budget price, you can't do much better than this deal. For this week only, Best Buy is offering an Acer Nitro 65 gaming PC with AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB graphics card for just $1,199.99 with free shipping. The RX 9060 XT graphics card is the superior 16GB VRAM variant that will run even the most recently released games smoothly at 60fps+ at up to 1440p.

Save $350 off Acer Nitro 65 RX 9060 XT (16GB) Gaming PC

Acer Nitro 65 AMD Ryzen 7 8700F Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB Gaming PC (16GB/1TB)

The Acer Nitro 65 is equipped with an air-cooled AMD Ryzen 7 8700F CPU, Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB NVMe SSD. The AMD Ryzen 7 8700F CPU is an 8-core, 16 thread processor with a max boost clock of 5GHz. It's a good CPU for gaming because of its high clock speed. It only has eight cores, but that's plenty for games since very few titles can benefit from more than eight or even six cores.

The Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB GPU is an excellent card for 1080p gaming

The Radeon RX 9060 XT graphics card comes in two variants, with the only difference between the two being the amount of VRAM: 8GB or 16GB. Unlike the vast majority of prebuilts which are equipped with the 8GB model, this particular system is equipped with the 16GB model. If you can afford it, you should only get the 16GB model. Numerous outlets ( including our own ) have demonstrated that the performance gap between the 8GB and 16GB models is significant.

The Radeon RX 9060 XT is an excellent GPU for 1080p gaming. It performs within range of the GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. The 16GB of VRAM also allows this GPU to hold its own in 1440p gaming, especially if you don't want to spend the extra hundreds of dollars more to upgrade to a more powerful card like the RX 9070 XT.

articles.title: Sauron Wears the One Ring and Battles the Balrog in New Rings of Power Season 3 Trailer
articles.summary: Prime Video has released a new trailer for the upcoming third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power that revealed more of the war to stop Sauron from forging the One Ring.
articles.body:
Prime Video has released a new trailer for the upcoming third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power that revealed more of the war to stop Sauron from forging the One Ring. You can watch the trailer via the player above or the embed below.

Season 3 is set several years after the events depicted in Season 2, picking up the story at the height of the War of the Elves.

While the new trailer features more looks at the Nazgnagôl, a Mûmakil, and fell beasts, the best is saved until last when Sauron dons the One Ring, which will allow him to bind all the peoples of Middle-earth to his will.

“I see the path to victory so certain,” Sauron says. “I will take my place as a conqueror, a sorcerer. A king. We have work to do.” These lines are spoken over footage of a Nazgnagôl getting the upper hand of Galadriel in a fight. (Sauron also seems to be getting into Galadriel’s head at one point as she dreams that he’s lying in bed next to her.)

It also appears Sauron will battle the Balrog at some point this season as the trailer shows a fiery battle. ( Simon Pegg voices the Balrog in the show.)

After the death of Celebrimbor in the Rings of Power Season 2 finale , Sauron is still seeking to forge the One Ring to rule them all as Season 3 begins. It would seem this season is going to see the Dark Lord come out on top in his quest to bring Middle-earth under his rule – well, for now anyway.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 debuts on Prime Video on November 11. In the meantime, read up on the show’s mysterious new orc character and learn why the Harfoots won’t be in Season 3 .

articles.title: Mass Effect 5 Was Supposed to Redeem the Series After Andromeda, and Now We'll Never Get That
articles.summary: I'm the sort of person that just replays my favorite games whenever there's a big gap between releases. And a decent amount of time, that's Mass Effect, whether it's just the first game or a run through the entire original trilogy. So, for me, a Mass Effect 5 that captured the magic of the first three games has been something I've been looking forward to since before it was even announced in 2021. Now that game will never exist.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece by Jackie Thomas, who has been playing and replaying Mass Effect for nearly 20 years now.

I'm the sort of person who replays my favorite games whenever there's a big gap between releases. And those favorites usually end up being from the Mass Effect series, whether it's just the first game or a run through the entire original trilogy. So, for me, a Mass Effect 5 that captured the magic of the first three games has been something I've been looking forward to since before it was even announced in 2020. Now, that game will never exist, thanks to EA closing down BioWare . And that f**king sucks.

When Mass Effect came out in 2007, I stood in line to get it on release night, and I played it incessently until I finished absolutely everything in it. I did the same thing when the second and third games came out, except I also played the previous games again ahead of time so everything would be fresh in my mind.

Ever since Mass Effect 3 came out, I've replayed the original games maybe a dozen times. I don't even drastically change the way I play Mass Effect each time I play it. Even after nearly 20 years of experiencing the original game, I still play an Adept every time, because pistols are OP and biotics are cool. And I still ultimately do a paragon playthrough, even when I tell myself that I'm going to be bad and play renegade. Mass Effect has felt like home to me for years, and it became my ultimate comfort game.

But eventually, Mass Effect Andromeda came out, and even though I tried to power through it, I ultimately gave up after a deluge of bugs and weird writing turned me off. I still haven't gone back and finished that game, but I still find myself downloading and playing Mass Effect when I run out of other games to play. Hell, with the amount of times I've played the first game, I can probably navigate most of its empty optional planets with my eyes closed. After today's news, I might just download it and play it again in solidarity.

You'd think that after getting burned on Mass Effect Andromeda, I would've learned my lesson. But in the years since Bioware teased what should have the fifth Mass Effect game, I let myself hope that it would redeem the series once again and land in that annual ME replay rotation.

And I know that after Anthem , and Dragon Age: The Veilguard's weird shift to a straight-up action game, I didn't have much of a reason to believe that Mass Effect 5 would have been this magical return to form. But I think what's hitting me the hardest about BioWare's closure is that we'll never know whether or not Mass Effect 5 would have been good.

The truth is, we didn't know much about the next Mass Effect game at all. Hell, I don't even know if it would have been called Mass Effect 5, but that's just easier to say than 'the next Mass Effect game' over and over again. Ever since it was announced, BioWare had been pretty quiet about the project, only really speaking up to reassure fans that it was still in development. And look how that turned out.

But some of the things that popped up about the game over the years did look pretty cool. Bioware showed off some concept art late last year, showing a Krogan civil war with a properly grizzled Krogan leading a whole squad of the grumpy lizards in a fight. I want to play that game.

Likewise, in one of the only teasers we ever got , the camera zooms through the galaxy, past what looks like the ruins of the Citadel, until it finally shows an older Asari climbing up some snowy ruins. And we don't see her full face, but even from the side, it sure looked like Liara. And, again, I'd love to revisit her character after she fully becomes an Asari Matriarch. But again, that game will never exist.

But there is at least hope that some games that are at least similar to Mass Effect are on the horizon. Just last year, Mass Effect director Casey Hudson's new studio announced Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic . I'm a huge Star Wars fan, so when that game comes eventually comes out, I'm sure I'll burrow my way into it like a tick and not come out for a week. But, just like Mass Effect 5, there's not a lot we know about Fate of the Old Republic quite yet. But at least Hudson has come out and said that it won't take until 2030 to release, so maybe we'll get it in 2029.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn is another one that I've had my eye on, and while I haven't really watched the show or read the books (even though both are on my list), I know that universe has a lot of potential for a Mass-Effect-Like. Then, there's Exodus , which is made by Wizards of the Coast of all companies, and has Mass Effect alumni working on it. The art style even makes it look like a Mass Effect game. Luckily, both of these titles seem like they're on track to actually come out next year, but only time will tell there.

As much as I'm earnestly looking forward to all three of those games, they're simply not Mass Effect. The aesthetics are there, the writing should be there, and it looks like the gameplay for Exodus at least is going to be quite good. And Fate of the Old Republic is a Star Wars game, and my love of Star Wars is what led me to play Mass Effect in the first place.

But no matter how good they end up being, I don't know if it's going to be as relaxing as hunting down all of the Keepers in the Citadel, and I probably won't be fighting a giant Reaper skeleton inside of a black hole. I am at least thankful that no matter how controversial Mass Effect 3's ending was, it was at least an ending . I would have loved another chapter and a chance to see whatever Bioware was cooking up with Mass Effect 5. But, at least I'll always have those first three games, and no amount of EA's mismanagement is going to take that away from me.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: EA Halts Development on Mobile Multiplayer Sims Game in Favor of Rumored Sims 4 Sequel
articles.summary: EA has paused development on a mobile multiplayer Sims game in favor of moving forward with a rumored Sims 4 sequel.
articles.body:
EA has paused development on a mobile multiplayer Sims game in favor of moving forward with a rumored Sims 4 sequel.

EA announced a wide variety of changes and projects today, including the closure of BioWare and the cancelation of Mass Effect 5 . It also seemed to lean into recent rumors that DICE and Respawn are making a new Star Wars Battlefront game . One other big change is that EA is shelving a mobile-first multiplayer Sims project, formerly known as Project Rene and now known as Project Lotus. The game was once envisioned as the next big Sims title , but plans changed to more of a mobile spin-off once EA saw that people were still hanging on to The Sims 4.

With that game being put on the back burner, EA is shifting its focus to a Sims title that it's calling Project Evergreen. Although EA hasn't revealed what the focus of this game will be, rumors have been swirling about this project for a some time now. The game, which was rumored to be under the codename Project X, is expected to be a sequel to The Sims 4. Now, here's where it may get a bit confusing: It's not The Sims 5. It's being viewed more like The Sims 4 2.0. I know, it is unnecessarily complicated.

As covered by Sims Community , the project is reportedly targeting September 2027 as its deadline to go gold, suggesting the game would launch in fall 2027. The game will release on PC and is also expected to be optimized for portable handhelds, such as the Steam Deck. If it really is releasing next year, we will likely hear more about it at The Game Awards or sometime in the first half of 2027.

Earlier this year, the team behind The Sims hinted at a new single-player game in the franchise for PC and console, noting that half of its development team was working on The Sims 4 and its "next evolution."

Ultimately, this sounds like a win for fans who have been hoping for a new traditional entry in the franchise. The Sims 4 was released in 2014, meaning it has been 12 years since the franchise got a new game. There are a ton of updates and expansions that keep the game fresh, but building something from scratch and moving away from all the bloat could be a strong move for the future of the series.

articles.title: VisionQuest Just Revealed a Connection to the First Captain America Movie... and Possibly Its Real Villain Too
articles.summary: Who is the Synthetic Man in VisionQuest? It turns out that J.I.M., aka the Human Torch, first showed up in Captain America: The First Avenger 15 years ago... and there may be much more to his story than we previously realized.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for VisionQuest through Episode 4.

In the latest episode of VisionQuest, “Malware,” the murderous synthezoid who has been lurking in the shadows and killing AI creators off is finally revealed to be Jocasta – aka Dr. Josephine Carrington. The character, played by T’Nia Miller, had only been referred to on the show as the “Butcherbird Killer” prior to this, but fans of the comics know all about Jocasta , the so-called Bride of Ultron! We’ve also known the character would be a part of VisionQuest, but there’s another android character mentioned in the episode who is perhaps a bit more of a surprise… or at least it’s a surprise how pivotal he may wind up being to the Disney+ series.

Yes, after 15 years, the MCU is finally getting around to dealing with the original Human Torch.

The Synthetic Man Is the Original Human Torch

The character was first teased in Captain America: The First Avenger all the way back in 2011. It was a blink-or-you’ll-miss-it moment during the 1943 Stark Expo scene where Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan) go on a double date. At one point, an exhibit can be glimpsed for “the Synthetic Man,” the creation of Dr. Phineas Horton. Encased in a glass case and seemingly deactivated, the Synthetic Man even had on the comics version of the Torch’s red costume. (And as any Marvel fan worth his weight in newsprint comics knows, this is a completely different character from Johnny Storm, the other Human Torch who is best known as a member of the Fantastic Four.)

Anyway, that was the last we saw or heard of the OG Torch… until now. Fans had pieced together that the character would be part of VisionQuest in some way, based on promo art featuring a man ablaze. That, combined with the Torch and Vision’s shared history in the comics, made it pretty clear that what was just a fun Easter egg in The First Avenger would now become something more meaningful and complete, as is the MCU’s way.

In “Malware,” Vision (Paul Bettany) and Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) attend a charity event dubbed “The Re-evolution of Man.” The gala is hosted by Mary McDonnell’s Dr. Katerina Wells, a former colleague of Josephine Carrington’s who, like Carrington, is also an expert on AI. Dr. Wells narrates a video presentation that is playing at the event, where she discusses the “ill-fated Synthetic Man” and explains a bit about his history. Later, she tells the assembled guests that Dr. Phineas Horton was the “grandfather of robotics” and that he was the creator of the Synthetic Man, also known as J.I.M. (notably, the Torch’s alter ego in the comics is Jim Hammond). The Synthetic Man’s source code, Wells explains, paved the way for all future artificial intelligence that followed. “He was the first of us,” the Vision says. “Miraculous, but flawed.”

We also learn that, unlike his comics counterpart, who was one of the original Marvel heroes and fought alongside Captain America and Namor in the super-group the Invaders during World War II, J.I.M. was deactivated after a series of “incendiary mishaps.” As Vision explains, “his inability to process complex emotions spun his clockwork too quickly, flooded his solar cells with oxygen until his entire being was consumed in fire.” Tommy responds, “You mean he felt to death?” Sad!

As for why this same problem never became an issue for the Vision, apparently the otherworldly power of the Mind Stone helped him to keep himself in check – and even though he no longer possesses the Stone in his new form, he still has enough of its residual power within his being. Why then did Ultron never suffer the same fate as the Synthetic Man/Human Torch? Could it be that his brief interaction with the Mind Stone’s power also affected him? (But then one must also ask, what about Jocasta…?)

At any rate, we now know that the Synthetic Man truly was also a Torch… though for now, anyway, it sounds as though that was a curse rather than a gift.

Is the Human Torch the Real Villain of VisionQuest?

While there are several apparent bad guys running around in VisionQuest right now, including Jocasta and Todd Stashwick’s Paladin, it’s clear that there’s still a Big Bad waiting in the background. Jocasta is traditionally portrayed as a good guy (she was an Avenger in the comics!), so she may flip sides soon, and a sympathetic backstory for Paladin is being planted as well – though since both characters have already killed in cold blood, it’s currently a bit difficult to see how they could be redeemed. But regardless, there’s also that ominous voice to consider of whoever it was who hired Paladin to track down Vision…

We’re halfway through VisionQuest at this point, so it seems likely that either the Human Torch or his creator, Dr. Horton, (or both) are being positioned to be behind that mysterious voice. Why else would VisionQuest give us so much information and backstory on the Torch? And if one of them is indeed the true villain of this series, the question then is why?

By the end of Episode 4, there’s also the matter of Ultron (James Spader) now having taken control of Vision’s body. That’s a dangerous situation to be sure, but VisionQuest has also hinted that there’s more to Ultron’s original design than we’ve previously known about. While E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire) figures out during this episode that the various Stark AIs have all been based on real people, Ultron insists that he is the exception. But is it possible that Dr. Horton and/or the Human Torch were somehow Ultron’s inspiration when he was created?

Of course, Tony Stark and Bruce Banner wouldn’t have consciously used either figure to base Ultron on, but don’t forget, Ultron just kind of came into existence on his own after the Science Bros thought they had failed. So something sparked Ultron into existence, but what? And is that same something now trying to track down its creation? VisionQuest is clearly about fathers and sons… so is Dr. Horton or the Torch Ultron’s actual father? We’ll find out soon enough.

articles.title: David Fincher Cut 60 Pages From Quentin Tarantino’s Cliff Booth Script
articles.summary: Quentin Tarantino penned the screenplay for The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, his follow-up to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, but he handed the directing reins over to David Fincher – who proceeded to cut about 60 pages from Tarantino’s screenplay.
articles.body:
Netflix has released a slew of new images from The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , which can be seen in the gallery below. Quentin Tarantino penned the screenplay for the film, which follows Brad Pitt’s former stuntman Cliff Booth in the years following Once Upon a Time in Hollywood .

But Tarantino isn’t behind the camera this time, handing the directing reins over to David Fincher – who proceeded to cut about 60 pages from Tarantino’s screenplay.

“The first draft I read was 230 pages. It was essentially two movies,” Fincher told Empire Magazine . “Somewhere in there was the Venn diagram of what Brad wanted to do, what I want to do, what Quentin wanted to do. Not ‘want to do,’ but the areas we would focus on.”

The trimmed down script nevertheless resulted in a movie that runs close to two hours and 20 minutes long.

Empire also interviewed Tarantino, who explained that his script for The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth “was very different” from the one he wrote for Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. “To me, it had the flavor of an Elmore Leonard paperback: a crime-story paperback feel,” the Oscar winner said.

The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth Images

Fincher added that he “liked the idea that it’s a story around a bonfire. … It wasn’t about the plot as much as it was about how the participants collided with one another in the back alleys of Hollywood in 1977.”

Tarantino's full story for The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will be published as a novel this December and is now available to preorder .

The Pulp Fiction filmmaker also recently revealed that he’s written the screenplay for his 10th and final film , but wants to “live” a little before actually making it. In the meantime, Tarantino has penned a swashbuckler comedy stageplay titled The Popinjay Cavalier, which will be produced in London’s West End next year with Sacha Baron Cohen starring in the lead role.

The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth opens in IMAX theaters globally on November 25, 2026 and launches on Netflix December 23, 2026. In addition to Brad Pitt, the film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Peter Weller.

articles.title: Star Wars: The Old Republic Fans Pay Their Respects to BioWare
articles.summary: EA shut down BioWare earlier today, and fans of Star Wars: The Old Republic are paying their respects to the beloved developer.
articles.body:
EA shut down BioWare earlier today , and fans of Star Wars: The Old Republic are paying their respects to the beloved developer.

Star Wars: The Old Republic was originally developed by BioWare, launching back in 2011. BioWare supported the MMO itself until 2023, when EA put Broadsword Games in charge of maintaining it. But the bulk of the game's story content was developed and written by BioWare, so it's little wonder that the SWTOR community would want to pay respects to the now-dormant studio following this latest news.

Reddit user WarlockingIn posted BioWare's farewell statement on the SWTOR subreddit , and in just a few hours, it's garnered nearly 5,000 upvotes and 742 comments supporting the now-defunct RPG developer.

Star Wars: The Old Republic - Shadow of Revan Gallery

Bae_the_Elf posted a comment , lamenting EA's treatment of the studio, saying, "RIP. One of the greatest gaming studios of all time in my opinion. Sad to see how corporate mismanagement and time sadly lead to the downfall of this studio. It would have been nice if they had just kept chugging out great RPGs at a steady pace for years."

Meanwhile, user AnnoyedYamcha was devastated by the closure, saying "NO. Not BIOWARE! They made so many great games. What the hell is going on!!! They were the bar for RPG's. KOTOR, MASS EFFECT, DRAGON AGE, JADE EMPIRE, they were all great! JADE EMPIRE though doesn't get enough love. I wish they made another. THANK YOU BIOWARE FOR EVERYTHING! 😭😭"

Some fans were surprised that SWTOR outlived BioWare, though. The top comment on the thread, from user Inangelion, simply says, "SWTOR outlives Bioware. What a strange timeline."

Some were even thankful that Broadsword took over, with user Dangerously_Stupid posting, "You know, a few years ago I was upset that BioWare was giving up SWTOR and handing it to Broadsword. I am no longer upset by that." Likewise, user KukiBreeze is just thankful that the MMO lives on another day, saying "Thank you Broadsword, a sh*tty day could have been 1000x sh*ttier otherwise."

Star Wars: The Old Republic fans aren't alone in mourning BioWare. People from across the internet have reacted to the studio's closure , and the fact that we'll never get a Mass Effect 5 . But, for now at least, Star Wars: The Old Republic lives on, with hundreds of hours of peak BioWare storytelling.

articles.title: Former BioWare Executive Producer Mark Darrah Says EA Might Be 'More Likely' to Sell IPs Like Mass Effect and Dragon Age After Studio’s Closure
articles.summary: Mark Darrah, who worked as an executive producer at BioWare from 1997 - 2021, shared his thoughts on the studio’s recent closure by EA and what he thinks might happen to its iconic IPs.
articles.body:
Mark Darrah, who worked as an Executive Producer at BioWare from 1997–2021, shared his thoughts on the studio’s recent closure by EA and what he thinks might happen to its iconic IPs.

EA announced a major restructuring in a lengthy statement on October 21. Amid some exciting developments for Sims, Fight Night, and Star Wars fans came the devastating news that BioWare — the studio responsible for beloved series like Mass Effect and Dragon Age — was being shut down .

“As we focus on these larger opportunities, we've had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect . We've made the decision not to move forward with this development, which means we’re closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace. BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly,” EA’s statement said.

Mass Effect: Commander John Shepard 1:6 Scale Statue - Photo Gallery

This news hit the gaming world hard , with fans taking to social media to mourn the developer and send fired staff their well-wishes. But one burning question has risen above the sadness: What does this mean for the future of BioWare’s IPs?

Some fans have urged EA to sell them off to other companies, with CD Projekt Red being a big favorite due to the two studios’ close relationship over the years. And while nothing is certain, Darrah shared some insight as to what’s possible for BioWare’s creations in the wake of this devastating development — and it’s cautiously optimistic.

“Remember BioWare is 100% owned by EA,” he said in a YouTube video . “EA owns all the IPs. They own Dragon Age, they own Mass Effect, they own Jade Empire. That doesn’t change the situation, really, at all. …Now, there’s nobody working on a [BioWare] game, or games, within the EA organization, and chances are there never will be, which might make them more likely to sell off those IPs. But it might also make them more likely to just try to forget that they ever existed and bury them in the vault.

“I think we still are gonna have to wait a little bit before we see if EA has any interest in selling off some of its dormant IPs. Right now, they seem to be in cost control mode. They might start into a revenue-generation mode where selling IPs might be more desirable.”

It’s worth mentioning that EA was acquired by a consortium of private investors back in August in a mind-boggling $55 billion deal. As part of this acquisition, the investment group was reportedly banking on the hope that artificial intelligence might help cut costs to help manage its debt.

Given the investment group’s massive debt, some fans are curious to know if this means selling off some of BioWare’s beloved IPs to other developers — or perhaps back to BioWare under a different brand. For now, nothing is certain, other than fans and fellow game developers are equally beside themselves as they grapple with the news that Mass Effect 5 might never get made.

articles.title: Mass Effect TV Series Remains Active at Prime Video Despite BioWare Closure
articles.summary: The Mass Effect video game franchise may have come to an end with the shocking demise of BioWare, but IGN can exclusively reveal that its future on the small screen remains possible. Sources inside Prime Video have confirmed that the Mass Effect television series remains in development at Amazon MGM Studios.
articles.body:
The Mass Effect video game franchise may have come to an end with the shocking demise of BioWare , but IGN can exclusively reveal that its future on the small screen remains possible. Sources inside Prime Video have confirmed that the Mass Effect television series remains in development at Amazon MGM Studios.

Our source added that, as of now, all the creatives who were attached to the TV project remain onboard.

As of August 2025, Doug Jung (Mindhunter, Star Trek Beyond) was serving as showrunner with Daniel Casey (Fast & Furious 9) writing the series. The production team also included Jessica Jones executive producer Karim Zreik, BioWare's Mass Effect boss Mike Gamble, and former Marvel Studios boss Ari Arad.

We learned last year that the show won’t retread Commander Shepard’s origin story from the games and will instead be set after the original trilogy.

Daniel Casey took to social media this past April to shoot down reports that Prime Video wanted rewrites to make the show more appealing to a non-gaming audience .

11 Mass Effect Characters and Moments the TV Show Needs to Be a Hit

The Mass Effect TV series had, at one point, been eyeing a Q4 2026 production start , but it remains without a release date as of time of this story’s publication.

Given the success of their Fallout TV series adaptation, Prime Video was reportedly hoping to capture lightning in a bottle twice with a Mass Effect show. IGN will keep you up to date on any further developments we learn.

Jim Vejvoda (he/him) is IGN's Assoc. Director of Entertainment Content.

articles.title: SonicFox Cancels Contract With Gaming Convention After Event Uses Likeness in AI-Generated Poster
articles.summary: Prolific fighting game player SonicFox has terminated their contract with a tournament in Norman, Oklahoma after organizers fed artwork of their mascot character into AI to generate a promotional poster for the event.
articles.body:
Prolific fighting game player SonicFox has terminated their contract with a convention in Norman, Oklahoma after organizers fed artwork of the pro's mascot character into AI to generate a promotional poster for the event.

SonicFox is one of the most successful fighting game players in the genre’s competitive scene. Known for being a multi-game specialist, SonicFox boasts multiple championships in a bevy of different titles, so it’s no surprise that they’re often invited as a special guest at tournaments across the United States.

One such tournament, taking place at a convention named Nexcon, invited SonicFox to attend alongside a few other notable guests. The convention is scheduled for November 14 - 15 in Norman, Oklahoma (home of the Sooners) — but now, SonicFox isn’t going to make an appearance.

On October 20, a concerned fan shared a promotional poster that Nexcon had made using generative AI on Twitter/X, which showed the likeness of SonicFox’s furry avatar, as well as the likenesses of other special guests, in an unmistakable AI art style.

“Not sure who’s in charge of Nexcon, but I absolutely refuse to have my likeness be AI-generated, and my interest in attending as a special guest has dropped to 0. Incredibly disrespectful,” the player replied .

It’s worth noting that much of the artwork SonicFox uses on their accounts is created by members of the furry community; feeding that artwork into a generative AI without their consent essentially steals their work to train on future models.

Not sure who’s in charge of Nexcon but I absolutely refuse to have my likeness be AI generated and my interest in attending as a special guest has dropped to 0. Incredibly disrespectful. — SonicFox (@SonicFox) October 20, 2026

Not sure who’s in charge of Nexcon but I absolutely refuse to have my likeness be AI generated and my interest in attending as a special guest has dropped to 0. Incredibly disrespectful.

Members of the fighting game community spoke up in support of SonicFox, with one summing up the prevailing sentiments in a reply : “Using AI to help promote an event that gathers creators and artists is pretty crazy.”

A day later, SonicFox announced that they had terminated their contract with the event, saying in a simple post that they are “no longer attending.”

At the time of writing, all mention of SonicFox has been removed from NexCon’s website. Fans are speaking out in support of the pro player, with many congratulating them for “standing on business.”

In other fighting game news, Roger Jr. gameplay footage for Tekken 8 was shown off at Evo France, and players finally got a first look at Yujiro Hanma’s in-game model before his arrival early next year.

articles.title: BioWare Was the Greatest RPG Developer Ever
articles.summary: There are many great role-playing game developers, past and present. But none can touch what BioWare has done over 30-plus years.
articles.body:
BioWare is dead , and my feelings are a strange cocktail of anger, sadness, and Jack’s Complete Lack of Surprise. The legendary RPG studio was bought by a private investment group earlier this year, and history shows that venture capital frequently kills what it touches, extracting whatever value out of it that it can before moving onto the next victim. It’s a hell of a contrast to the beginning of BioWare, which started out as such a pure thing. Two practicing doctors, Ray Muzyka and Greg Zeschuk, quit medicine to pursue their dream of making computer role-playing games. Sure, the studio was bought and sold a couple of times between then and now, and yes, BioWare’s recent results haven’t lived up to its venerable past, but my goodness, what a legacy this studio leaves behind.

Everyone knows Baldur’s Gate now on account of Larian Studios’ Game of the Year-winning, 10 out of 10 Baldur’s Gate 3 from 2023, but what younger gamers might not know is that the first two Baldur’s Gate RPGs were built by BioWare in the late ‘90s. While they weren’t the studio’s first games – that honor goes to the 1996 mech action-sim Shattered Steel – they were the two that put BioWare on the map. Each was an incredibly deep and sprawling RPG based on the Dungeons & Dragons ruleset that was good for upwards of 200 hours of gameplay. At the time, they reset the bar for what a CRPG could be. Let me put it this way: Baldur’s Gate 1 took home IGN’s Game of the Year award in 1998 … over Half-Life . That’s how good Baldur’s Gate was.

BioWare: Stories and Secrets From 25 Years of Game Development - Exclusive Book Preview

After another action-game pitstop in the form of 2000’s excellent MDK2, BioWare returned to role-playing with Neverwinter Nights, another CRPG that arguably brought video games closer to the pen-and-paper, pizza-party-at-your-best-friend/DM’s-house version of D&D than any game before it. It was the runner-up for IGN’s Best Role-Playing Game of 2002, finishing behind just one game: a little project you might have heard of called The Elder Scrolls 3: Morrowind.

Up to this point, BioWare had primarily been known in PC circles as a prominent CRPG developer. And then Microsoft made a deal with the studio and LucasArts to develop an exclusive new Star Wars RPG for the fledgling Xbox console. You already know what the result was: the absolutely unimpeachable Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, which happens to be my personal favorite role-playing game of all time. My biases aside, it is unquestionably one of the best RPGs ever made. It’s also a lock for top-3 Star Wars games of all-time, and it has a strong case for No. 1 on that list. It told an incredible story in Star Wars’s ancient past and truly let you embrace the Light Side or Dark Side of the Force. I went fully evil just because KOTOR let me do so! And not only that, it embraced those choices. At one point, I distinctly remember triple-crossing someone – double-crossing the guy that I’d already double-crossed. Its plot twist is legendary, and on the off chance that the long-in-development-hell remake ever comes out, I won’t spoil it for you here. But whether it was visiting plenty of planets (including Kashyyk!), bonding with your party members (shout-out to my favorite droid, HK-47!), or planning out my evil Force attacks by stacking up my attacks in the turn-based combat system, KOTOR was the ultimate pairing of a beloved IP and an industry-leading developer.

Another Xbox console exclusive followed, albeit from a different team within BioWare. While KOTOR director Casey Hudson was planning something even bigger for his team’s next project, another crew at BioWare delivered the sublime and historically underrated Jade Empire, which was steeped in Chinese mythology. IGN gave it a 9.9 out of 10 (on a 100-point scale!) back in 2005, and while it was nowhere near the commercial success KOTOR was, it was every bit as big a hit with critics and fans.

And then came Mass Effect. BioWare promised us a space opera – a trilogy in which our choices in each game would carry over to the next and ultimately affect the ending to the whole story. Microsoft had wisely signed it as a console exclusive, and boy oh boy did it pay off. Mass Effect was one of the core memories most people have about the Xbox 360. It was released in fall of 2007, the greatest stretch in Xbox and quite possibly gaming history – and it actually delivered on its space-opera promise. As your custom Commander Shepard, the first in the trilogy introduced us to the universe and humanity’s place within it – including Shepard’s path to becoming a galaxy-protecting Spectre. It introduced the Reapers, and so many phenomenal companion characters from Wrex to Garrus to Liara among many others. And like KOTOR, it too allowed you to be a Paragon of good or a Renegade of evil. (And yes, I once again tested the limits of how bad BioWare would allow me to be.)

The first is my personal favorite of the trilogy, but for many that honor goes to Mass Effect 2, which leveled up your relationship with Shepard’s companions and more or less built the entire campaign around them. As promised, your save file imported into the sequel, bringing with it your Shepard’s look and choices from the first game. It also evolved Mass Effect’s gameplay from light turn-based, semi-tactical combat to more of a pure third-person cover shooter while sacrificing none of its role-playing elements.

The controversial trilogy-capper is best remembered for its ending, which upset fans so much that BioWare tried to improve it in a post-launch patch. But forgotten alongside that is how great the rest of it was. It took the time to really let you – and your Shepard – say goodbye to the friends you’d made along the way (or at least, the ones you hadn’t chosen to kill or sacrifice), and its combat was improved further over Mass Effect 2, making Mass Effect 3 a truly world-class third-person shooter alongside its well-established role-playing bonafides.

Whatever your thoughts of Mass Effect 3’s ending, BioWare had done what they said they’d do: They built a three-game space opera that spanned more than 100 hours of gameplay over the course of the five years it took to get all three games out the door. We developed meaningful bonds with its characters, in part because they’d been written so well. It was a bold RPG experiment, and one that, for my money, hasn’t been replicated or even attempted since.

The Mass Effect trilogy was, in hindsight, probably BioWare’s peak by just about any measure, but the studio kept going. Another original IP, Dragon Age, saw four RPGs released over a decade and a half – with the third of those, 2014’s Dragon Age Inquisition, taking home IGN’s Game of the Year Award . Anthem was a bold but ultimately unsuccessful attempt to bring BioWare’s storytelling talents to the hot-at-the-time live-service space. The studio cleaned Mass Effect up nicely for an excellent remaster of the trilogy in 2021 after the BioWare Montreal team’s disappointing Mass Effect Andromeda in 2017. Heck, BioWare even made a full-blown RPG starring Sonic in a team-up with Sega in 2008’s Sonic Chronicles: The Dark Brotherhood!

And after announcing a fifth Mass Effect game that fans hoped would redeem the series after Andromeda, that project is now canceled alongside the studio being shut down. As sad as this day is – for both fans and BioWare employees who were there at any point during its 31-year history – I am left with a fulfilling sense of gratitude to this studio for all of the memorable gaming experiences it’s given me. With respect to CD Projekt Red, Larian, and Bethesda Game Studios, there’s never been a better RPG developer over a longer period of time than BioWare. It won’t be forgotten.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Chris Pratt Reaffirms Star-Lord Will Return in the MCU and Plans Are Being Made Right Now
articles.summary: Chris Pratt has confirmed that Star-Lord's return to the MCU is actively being figured out.
articles.body:
Chris Pratt has confirmed that Star-Lord's return to the MCU is actively being figured out.

The beloved galactic hero has been absent from the MCU since 2023, but his last appearance ended with a promise during the credits: Star-Lord will return. When speaking with The Playlist , Chris Pratt was asked about Star-Lord's future. Pratt confirmed that Marvel has been having conversations about bringing back the character, but he's remaining tight-lipped on when that will happen.

“I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” he explained. “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.”

Of course, Avengers: Doomsday is right around the corner and has a stacked cast... but Pratt is not among the list of confirmed stars. There are some actors who are heavily rumored to appear , but haven't been officially announced. However, Pratt hasn't really been part of the rumor mill. It's possible that he will be in the film's sequel, Avengers: Secret Wars , but we will likely have to wait until next year to know for sure.

Director James Gunn has been open about having no plans to do another Guardians of the Galaxy film , especially since he is now heading up DC Studios. Still, many of the characters he adapted for the big screen still live on in the MCU. Perhaps Star-Lord will get his own TV series. Maybe a solo film... or maybe he will return with a new crew in a potential Guardians of the Galaxy 4, helmed by another director. There are a ton of possibilities, but you can rest assured knowing Star-Lord is coming back.

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Review So Far
articles.summary: This bigger and better version of DMZ makes a great first impression.
articles.body:
This is a standalone review that covers only Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ mode. You can find our campaign review here , with multiplayer impressions to follow after launch.

Extraction shooters feel a little like a modern trend, with some heavy hitters like Marathon and Arc Raiders shaking the table within the last year or so, but they’ve been a growing experiment in the shooter space for the past decade or so. Call of Duty dabbled in it with the original DMZ back in 2022 (you could argue they were late to the party then), and its return in 2026 is timely. But with so much high quality competition on the market, is it welcome? I’ve only dipped my toe in since its “pay to play on time” launch on Tuesday – about five or so hours of vehicle hijacking, SAM site hacking, and target elimination on my docket so far – but this bigger, better DMZ makes a great first impression.

The PvPvE dynamic of extraction shooters often lives and dies by how well the mission and level design encourages you to explore, rewards you for overcoming challenges, and guides you to interact with others in order to keep those spoils. The fictional Korean Hajin region your exploits take place in is well suited for this. Its dense pockets of urban development – a village in the north, the dangerous main city in the east, an isolated prison out west – are separated by rocky forests concealing all sorts of militarized checkpoints and other points of interest hiding loot to shove into your pockets. Parts of it look a little samey, the consequence of modern urban development where (at least from the outside) most buildings look the same, especially compared to some of DMZ’s big sci-fi competition that go above and beyond to look striking at first glance.

The map is so big that you could spend the entirety of your approximately half-hour runs in only a fraction of it. Battle Royales (like CoD’s own Warzone) move players around by having an encroaching death cloud forcing everyone into a smaller and smaller area. DMZ instead entices squads to adventure with its Dynamic Operations.

Dynamic Ops are spontaneous missions that appear as you travel across the battlefield which come in lots of forms, from securing a package to blowing up a target to escorting a VIP. Many of them are multi-stage affairs that have your fireteam moving from point to point as NPC enemies ramp up a more coordinated defense against you. These all get rewarded by supply drops that grant you loot, the value of which escalates based on how many of them you're successfully completing. I prefer this sort of objective chasing to the more standard task lists in other games like this (which also exist here, in fairness) because it makes for more engaging individual runs. I’ll prepare the best I can beforehand, but can’t be ready for every possible string of operations once I deploy.

There are many actions and events, like aforementioned supply drops, that are broadcast to everyone within earshot, hypothetically to tempt other players to be nosy (and potentially belligerent), but my skirmishes with others have been pretty limited so far. It’s still technically the early access period, so a wave of operators is set to crash against me in the coming days, but I found that most people have opted to mind their own business. It would be a mistake to confuse this passivity with pacifism though – this isn’t the Arc Raiders playerbase, which spent many of the opening months of that game more interested in helping than hurting. Whenever another player was in eye or earshot, it was assumed that a fire fight was to follow. It’s just unclear at this point how much of that was motivated by them wanting what I had versus just coincidentally being in the same place at the same time.

Hajin is also a pretty lively place. Enemy patrols speed down roadways, sometimes as lone jeeps and other times in large caravans. Helicopters and drones streak across the skies looking for interlopers like me, or occasionally other NPCs from rival factions tearing the map apart. A train runs on a schedule, and you can absolutely hitch a ride on it to get from place to place. Squads of enemies could be posted up anywhere. Weird exploding robot dogs can sniff you out as you slink from building to building. There was always at least a base level of tension with every step I took or round I let off, because there was just enough going on around me that any push I made could be the one that knocks over the house of cards I was hiding behind.

Clashes with the NPC denizens of the DMZ start pretty tame, but ramp up as you and your squad make yourself more notorious by killing enemies and completing objectives. As enemy units start to don armor, pull up in more durable vehicles, and use higher grade weaponry to take you down, fire fights can get desperate quickly. There's an instinct for people in pick-up groups to run out on their own, potentially to get first dibs on loot perhaps, and they almost always regret it – it doesn’t take much for enemies to get the drop on you, as you are only where you are and they are potentially anywhere and everywhere else.

Call of Duty’s top tier military shooter gunplay, toeing the line between the lethality of simulations and the snappy speed of arcadey romps, feels at home in DMZ as well. All of the new tweaks, like the way your weapons interact with your surroundings or movement adjustments, feel like it had roaming gunfights in an open world in mind. Being able to cancel out of mantles so you aren’t stuck in an animation when you least want to be feels like the kind of quality of life inclusion that Warzone demonstrated was needed for a long time. That said, the smattering of guns lack much in the way of real identities outside of the normal archetypal framings that have existed in gaming forever (shotgun, assault rifle, sniper, etc.).

You can also drop into story missions, which are quest chains that include more structure, resembling the campaign missions without the more cinematic story elements. These were pretty rowdy and unique, like an escort mission where our squad had to wheel an injured general out of hospital, bed and all, while enduring swarms of enemy combatants. There's a finite number of these and the possible rewards are more limited, with less incentive to explore the places around you and no enemy players to pirate or evade. But they serve as a great tasting platter of the pace Dynamic Ops keep and a good tour of the various locations you'll need to get familiar with on the map.

In between missions, you tend to all of your gear and progression from the safety of your FOB. Weapons, crafting ingredients, and consumables that you procure out in the field can be sorted through here, all of it put at risk when you equip it and redeploy. When you unlock the 3D printer and gunsmith areas, crafting new toys and upgrading weapons becomes the main way you spend your plunder to enhance your chances in Hajin. The value proposition of spending in-game money on upgrades is still hard to parse for me this early on. You can easily blow tens of thousands of won to trick out a weapon, but there hasn't been an obvious benefit to doing so that outweighs the risk of throwing all of that hard earned money down the drain if you die while using it. That’s the kind of knowledge that only comes with reps, I imagine.

Similarly, Operators have individual sets of trait trees that you upgrade with points they earn in the field. These don’t appear to be novel to any individual fighter; there's no Ghost-specific ability where he gets unique buffs while saying something very British. Instead there are pools of passive traits across three categories, all operators have a choice between the same handful of major traits, while the 15 or so minor traits that fill out the trees are randomized. What makes an operator special seems to be limited mostly to how they look and sound, which was a bit of a bummer.

These traits can be pretty meaningful in the field, though. One of the randomized traits I acquired for Valeria, Ammo Scavenger, doubled the ammo I got from ammo packs and made conserving my shots basically a thing of the past. The faster revive speed all operators have access to in their Survivalist tree has been the difference between clutch plays and total wipes on more than one occasion. There's definitely some kind of character building to be had here, but you really can’t know where it’s all leading until the next group of traits to choose from are revealed. And all that is before accounting for the fact that I'm not sure there's a way to reset or reallocate these trait points outside of abandoning the operator all together if you fail to extract with them (as opposed to spending some cash to get them back into the fight).

My first steps into the new Korean War have been intense so far, and I know I’ve only scratched the surface. Hajin is a region brimming with promise, even if most of it has the kind of design you have to live in for awhile to be able to find its unique charms. There are zones I’ve yet to see and some secrets I'm sure to encounter while I stalk, slide, and shoot my way through it. I’m sure it will get rowdier as the general public starts to pile into the servers on launch day, but for now I really dig the emphasis on the E in the PvPvE structure of these runs. Dynamic Operations have kept me moving and earning, while the factions at war in the region buzz around the map, at first dutifully watching their posts and eventually doggedly hunting me down.

I’m just as eager to spend more time out in the field as I am with my nose in the menus of gunsmithing and operator leveling to tease out what nuance there can be found between the battle. I’ll be back with my final, scored review of DMZ once I’ve done a whole lot more of both.

One of the most iconic fast food restaurants from the GTA universe is becoming real ahead of GTA 6's release.

articles.title: Dodgers Lack Of Situational Hitting Cost Them In The Playoffs
articles.summary: The Dodgers' failure to move runners over or score them with less than two outs has been their Achilles' heel and cost in them their NLCS series against the...
articles.body:
They were old , they were tired, they were outplayed , they were outmanaged. The foregoing represents a sampling of answers to the question of why the Los Angeles Dodgers' dynasty seemingly ended when the Milwaukee Brewers swept them to win the National League pennant.

All of the above are true. At 30.8 years of age, the Dodgers sported the oldest roster in the game. Los Angeles has played 350 games in four countries, over the past two years. Pat Murphy pulled all the right levers, and Dave Roberts did not .

But one of the main culprits has been the Dodgers' Achilles' heel for many years – situational hitting. Some of the stats belie this idea. For instance, Los Angeles hit .262 with runners in scoring position this season (see all the way at the bottom), which was seventh in all of MLB. And their rate of "productive outs"* was 28%, when league average was just 28.7%. Los Angeles scored a league-average 51.2% of runners from third base with less than two outs. And they were above the league average of 52.2% with regard to advancing a runner from second with no outs (53.5%).

*Productive outs are advancing a runner with none out or driving in a runner with the second out of an inning.

But if you watch the Dodgers day-to-day, and if you watched them in the playoffs, you know what you saw, and you know that numbers lie. For instance, you know that the Dodgers had the 8 th fewest sacrifice attempts all season (just 27, while the Tampa Rays, who are about to play in the World Series, had 82). When asked in his press conference following Game 3 of the NLCS about his failure to bunt the leadoff baserunner over with Tommy Edman at the plate both times, Roberts said he wanted to play for the big inning.

Maybe Roberts didn't trust Edman insofar as he attempted a sacrifice bunt in Game 2 of the Division Series and popped it up. Maybe it was just bad timing, as Will Smith came to the plate with two on and no outs in the fifth inning of that same game, and flew out to right (Smith has never bunted in his eight-year career).

But it isn't just the managerial decisions. As with Edman's inability to get the bunt down, it is the players' failure to execute when the lights are the brightest. To wit:

Trailing 1-0 in the second inning of Game 4 of the Division Series, Shohei Ohtani led off with a walk, stole second, and went to third when catcher Sean Murphy threw the ball into left field, all while Teoscar Hernández struck out. With one out, slugger Max Muncy came to the plate just needing to pull a ground ball or hit a fly ball, and the game would have been tied. Instead, he hit a pop up less than 200-feet to short. Fortunately for the Dodgers, Mauricio Dubón dropped the ball, allowing Ohtani to score the tying run.

In Game 1 of the NLCS, Muncy struck again. At the plate in a 0-0 game with Ohtani on second and Hernández on first with no outs, Muncy struck out. Pages followed with an RBI single, and then Kyle Tucker walked to load the bases with one out. Kiké Hernández came to the plate needing to loft a fly ball to extend the lead. Instead, he grounded into an inning-ending double-play. That would be the Dodgers' lone run in their eventual 2-1 loss.

Move ahead to Game 3, which was essentially a "must win" after losing the first two in Milwaukee. Los Angeles found themselves down 1-0 in the sixth inning, when Teoscar Hernández and Tucker led off with walks. And that man, Muncy, again came to the plate and again struck out. After an Ohtani walk loaded the bases, Smith doubled two home to give the Dodgers the lead. But with runners on second and third and one out, Kiké Hernández and Edman both struck out, ending the threat. Those would be the only two runs the two-time defending champs would score in their 6-2 loss.

Game 4 was a most perfect ending to this era of Dodgers baseball. Down 0-3 with their backs against the wall, Los Angeles got two runners on with one out in the first and chance to set the tone. Rather, Smith grounded into an inning-ending double-play.

In the second, Tucker and Teoscar Hernández both singled. Rather than keeping Miguel Rojas in the game for a sacrifice attempt, Roberts called on Muncy off the bench, who promptly struck out. The inning worked out okay, as Pages singled home a run and Ohtani hit a massive three-run homer to stake the Dodgers to a 4-0 lead.

In the home half of the sixth, trailing 5-4, Muncy again struck out; this time with a runner on third and two outs.

The next inning, things were going according to plan. Still chasing a run, Pages led off with a double and Kiké Hernández bunted him to third (maybe Roberts learned his lesson from Game 3). Dodger Stadium was rocking at Ohtani came to the plate. Three pitches later he had struck out. And when Betts grounded out to short, the tying run was left on third yet again.

In the eighth, Smith hit a double down the right field line with one out. Sal Frelick misplayed it, allowing Smith to move to third. Up came Tucker – the highest paid player in baseball this season at $60 million. A fly ball would even the score and keep the Dodgers' hopes alive for at least another inning. On the second pitch he saw, Tucker hit a ball 217-feet to short center field that Garrett Mitchell sprinted into to catch, running the ball all the way back to the infield to keep Smith standing on third. Teoscar Hernández struck out, leaving the tying run on third base for the third inning in a row, which effectively ended the season and the dynasty.

It is accurate to say that the Dodgers need to get younger and quicker. But it is even more accurate to say that the Dodgers need to get better – better at doing the small things that flip innings, flip games, flip series. They need to move runners up 90-feet; they need to score runners from third with less than two outs; and they need to do all of these things in the post-season, when runs are at a premium, and games are decided by the slimmest of margins*. And if they want to learn how, they should simply tune in to the World Series that starts Friday night, as both the Rays and the Brewers are experts at playing that way.

*Los Angeles hit .116 with runners in scoring position this post-season. Milwaukee (so far) is hitting .284.

articles.title: Brandon Sanderson Wants to Know Who Really Wrote the Mr. Beast Book
articles.body:
Brandon Sanderson, author of The Cosmere books , has some thoughts on the new Mr. Beast book. More specifically, he is wondering who the true author actually is. During the latest episode of his podcast , Intentionally Blank, he decided to dive into his own perception of The Most Dangerous Games.

"I'm really curious who the ghost writer was," said Sanderson. "I would love for them to be credited, but I can see why they're not." He then goes on to explain how he personally goes about co-authoring books, which he recently did with Blightfall, and how he thinks that differs from being an editor. His final point on the matter was "if you see someone else's name on a book, chances are I came up with the outline and then was the editor on it."

For anyone who has followed Mr. Beast's YouTube career, it seems pretty unlikely that he did any of the writing himself. The fact that James Patterson is also listed on the book would make it seem the famous author is likely the one who did all of the heavy lifting to get this story off the ground. But Sanderson questions just how involved Patterson actually was in this project and if the true author is maybe left uncredited.

"Normally it's James Patterson and somebody," explains Sanderson, "what happens in those situations usually is James Patterson has an idea, they brainstorm and outline together, then the person writes the book and Patterson reads it and offers feedback."

"It doesn't feel like a James Patterson book," continues Sanderson. "but it's very strange for Patterson to use an uncredited ghostwriter, right?"

As someone who has helped finish The Wheel of Time Book series for Robert Jordan, Sanderson is no stranger to co-authoring a story. He admits later in the podcast that it's certainly possible that Patterson could have written the book, but he thinks an uncredited ghostwriter was definitely involved.
